 Two surfaces show tournament standings — the pinned Discord board and the public league page — and this makes both readable, and both ranked correctly while a round is still being played.

 Ranking

 Standings update live, so the board compares teams that have played different numbers of rounds. Points alone put a 2-1 team and a 2-2 team in the same bucket: in the current league that placed a 2-2 team at rank 10 above three 2-1 teams, and stranded a 2-1 team at 23 below eight of them.

 Within an equal-points group, fewest rounds played now ranks first — a team that reached those points in fewer rounds still has one in hand. Rounds played rather than losses, because the two diverge the moment a draw exists: at equal points 0-0-3 carries no losses despite having spent three rounds, and would outrank 1-1-0.

 Ranking on match-win percentage instead was considered and rejected. It orders the top identically and wrecks the bottom, where the 1/3 floor collapses 1-2, 1-3, 0-2, 0-3 and 0-4 onto a single value and a winless team outranks teams that have won. Used inside an equal-points group, rounds played never reaches the floor.

 The Discord board

 Rows were proportional text, so nothing lined up and the first real tiebreak was invisible:

 11. **Brion Stoutarm** — 6 pts (2-1-0)

 Now each row is an inline code span holding rank, points, record and OMW%, followed by the name in normal markdown:

 ` 8 9 3-1 52.1%` **gypsy caravan**
────────── **top 8 cut** ──────────
` 9 9 3-1 50.0%` **CFB**
`25 3 1-2 63.9%` ~~LED Soundsystem~~ *(dropped)*

 A fenced block would align but strip markdown, costing a dropped team its strikethrough. An inline span does both: equal character counts render equal widths, so every name starts at the same x, while the name stays outside the span. The numbers lead because the parts whose rendered width cannot be known — emoji in a team name, a name long enough to wrap — have to come last. Discord draws emoji inside a code block as an image of non-integer character width, so a name like 🐄 🤣 Juumi's Lil LOLcow🤣 🐄 cannot be padded into line at all.

 Column widths are measured from the teams being shown, so a drawn record ( W-L-D , two wider than W-L ) or a three-digit rank widens a column instead of knocking every row below it out of true.

 The cut rule is drawn after the rank cut_after_rank gives, not after cut_to . A dropped team keeps its standings place — its record still feeds every opponent's tiebreak — but cannot be seated, so drawing at cut_to would promise the last bracket seat to a team that cannot take one. No rule is drawn when the cut cannot be filled, matching start_playoff 's own refusal.

 The league page

 New tournament tab: standings, pairings and rosters, with dropped teams marked and the cut line drawn from the same function Discord uses. It keeps rank-then-name column ordering — it has real table columns, where the constraint that forces numbers first on Discord does not apply.

 Both surfaces read get_standings_with_omw , which returns the ranking and the OMW map from one load, so the figure printed is the figure sorted on rather than a second derivation that can drift. TournamentParticipant.record is the single definition of the W-L format, and keeps the draw count when one was actually recorded.

 Known follow-ups, not included

 get_final_placement feeds payout and inherits the new tiebreak. A team that drops mid-swiss with its final match unreported can now sort above an active team it previously tied with. Narrow — it needs an unreported match at finish, which count_unreported_matches already warns about — but it is a behaviour change outside the display layer.

 omw and cut_after reach create_standings_embed as optional arguments that default to rendering the old board, so the invariant is enforced by each of four call sites remembering two keywords rather than by the signature.

 The league page payload carries record as a formatted string and never match_wins / match_losses as numbers, so the page cannot split W from L or sort on wins without re-parsing it.

 aberdasher 

 added 14 commits
 September 20, 2026 01:52 

 DraftBot: expose swiss OMW% as its own function 

 …

 2e69ad3 

 rank_standings computed the opponents' match-win percentages it sorts by and
threw them away. omw_percentages returns that map, and rank_standings now sorts
by it, so a caller that has to show the tiebreak reads the same numbers the
sort used instead of reimplementing them.

 DraftBot: build the league site's standings, pairings and roster payload 

 …

 83baacd 

 league_site_data assembles one JSON payload for the public league page: every
team with its captain and roster, the ranked standings with their OMW%
tiebreak, and every round's pairings with scores where they have been reported.
It is injected into league_site/index.html at publish time, so the page is a
single self-contained file and the copy in the working tree carries nobody's
roster.

Standings come from get_standings_data and the tiebreak from omw_percentages,
the same two functions the Discord standings embed uses, so the public page
cannot disagree with it about who is winning.

Captains are the one roster slot with no name of their own: the roster table
excludes them by design, and Discord renders them as a mention. PlayerStats is
keyed by guild and does not cover them either -- 15 of the live league's 40
captains had never drafted in that guild -- so names fall back through signup
history, this guild before any other, which names all but one of them.

 DraftBot: skip the league page check where the page is not checked out 

 …

 1d46127 

 league_site/ is git-excluded, so the test that proves index.html still has an
injectable payload block only has a file to read on a machine that carries the
site.

 DraftBot: drop the draw count from the league standings record 

 …

 071cb68 

 Every team match has to produce a winner, so the third number was zero on
every row. It is still appended when it is non-zero: the schema permits a draw
even though the rules do not, and a record that had one must not silently
lose it.

 DraftBot: drop the draw count from the Discord standings too 

 …

 8fd38ee 

 The standings embed rendered W-L-D, where the draw is zero on every row: every
team match has to produce a winner, and an even team size that ends level is
decided by a representative playoff rather than left drawn.

The format now lives as TournamentParticipant.record, which the embed and the
public league page both read. The page had grown its own copy a commit ago;
one definition is what stops the two from disagreeing. A non-zero draw is
still shown, because the column exists and set_result can write to it.

 DraftBot: say on the league page who has dropped 

 …

 abf1fca 

 A dropped team keeps its place and its record, because both still count towards
the tiebreaks of every team it played. Unmarked on the public page that reads as
a bug: the team sits in the standings while the pairings quietly stop including
it, and a reader has no way to tell who is still being paired. The Discord board
already says so; the page did not.

The flag rides on the team rather than the standings row because the pairings
resolve a team through the same id, so a marker kept on the standings row would
leave a dropped team unmarked in half the places it appears.

 DraftBot: put the league page's cut line where the bracket will fall 

 …

 ba28364 

 The line was drawn after the row whose rank equals cut_to, which counts dropped
teams. A dropped team holds its rank -- its record still feeds every opponent's
tiebreak -- but _cut_eligible will not seat it, so once a team inside the cut
drops, the line promises the last seat to a team that cannot take it.

_cut_eligible is imported rather than restated, private though it is. "Who can
be seated" is the bot's rule, and a second copy of it here is exactly the kind
of divergence between the public page and Discord this module exists to prevent.

No line at all when the cut cannot be filled: start_playoff refuses that cut
outright, so drawing one would advertise a bracket that will not run.

 DraftBot: rank a team with a round in hand above one that lost it 

 …

 545740e 

 Standings update live, so the board compares teams that have played different
numbers of rounds. Two teams on 6 points are not equal when one is 2-1 with a
round outstanding and the other is 2-2: the first cannot yet have lost twice,
and ranking it below the second reads as the board being broken. In the current
league that put a 2-2 team at rank 10 above three 2-1 teams, and stranded a 2-1
team at 23 below eight of them.

Losses sort ahead of OMW% rather than replacing points with match-win
percentage. MWP would order the top of the table identically and wreck the
bottom: the 1/3 floor collapses 1-2, 1-3, 0-2, 0-3 and 0-4 onto one value, so a
winless team would outrank teams that have won a match.

 DraftBot: show OMW% on the standings board 

 …

 c0106e7 

 OMW% is the first real tiebreak and decides most of the order once points and
losses are level, but the board never showed it -- the number was computed for
the sort and discarded, leaving rows that look arbitrarily ordered.

The mapping is passed in rather than rebuilt in the renderer. Deriving it needs
the match graph, and a second derivation is how the figure on the board drifts
from the figure that ordered it. Callers without one render exactly as before.

 DraftBot: line the standings board up without losing its formatting 

 …

 3ef8608 

 The board was a run of proportional text, so nothing aligned: points and OMW%
landed wherever the team name before them happened to end. A fenced code block
aligns but strips markdown, which would cost a dropped team its strikethrough.

An inline code span does both. It renders monospace, so spans built to the same
character count render the same width and every name starts at the same x --
and the name stays outside the span, where bold and strikethrough still apply.
The numbers have to lead: they are the fixed-width anchor, and the parts whose
rendered width cannot be known here, emoji in a team name or a name long enough
to wrap, must come last so their drift never reaches the columns. Discord draws
emoji in a code block as an image of non-integer character width, so a name
like '🐄 🤣 Juumi's Lil LOLcow🤣 🐄' cannot be padded into line at all.

Column widths come from the teams being shown rather than being fixed, so a
drawn record (W-L-D, two wider than W-L) or a three-digit rank widens the
column instead of knocking every row below it out of true. OMW% is five wide
because 100.0 is a character longer than 99.9.

The public league page keeps name-second ordering: it has real table columns,
where the constraint that forces numbers first here does not apply.

get_standings_with_omw returns the ranking and the tiebreak from one load, so
the figure displayed is the figure sorted on rather than a second derivation.
Without it the board renders the new layout with the column silently missing,
which is what the standings-message test now pins.

 DraftBot: move the cut line's rank out of the league page module 

 …

 1975b29 

 Where the top-N line falls is not a property of the public page. It is the
bot's rule about who a cut can seat -- a dropped team keeps its standings place
because its record still feeds every opponent's tiebreak, but cannot take a
bracket seat -- and the Discord board is about to draw the same line.

Lifted beside _cut_eligible, which it already depended on, so both surfaces
read one definition rather than Discord growing a second copy that agrees with
the page until the week a dropped team climbs into the cut.

 DraftBot: draw the cut line on the standings board 

 …

 7599655 

 The board ranked forty teams with nothing to say which eight of them were
playing for a bracket seat, so the only way to read the cut was to count.

Drawn after the rank cut_after_rank gives rather than after cut_to: those part
company the moment a dropped team sits above the line, and drawing at cut_to
would promise the last seat to a team that cannot take one. That function also
declines to draw at all when the cut cannot be filled, because start_playoff
refuses such a cut outright.

The rule carries its label instead of being a bare line. Field values split
between rows at Discord's 1024-character cap, so with a larger cut the rule can
land at the top of a continuation field, away from the rank it follows.

 DraftBot: rank on rounds played, not on losses 

 …

 0a69138 

 Losses stood in for "has a round in hand", and the two part company the moment
a draw exists -- which _apply_result records whenever a team match ends level.
At equal points, 0-0-3 has spent three rounds and carries no losses, so it
outranked 1-1-0, which has spent two and still has one to play: exactly the
comparison the tiebreak was added to get right, inverted. Rounds played is the
quantity the reasoning was always about, and it is already computed one
function above as the denominator of mwp().

Ranking on match-win percentage instead would order the top identically and
wreck the bottom, where the 1/3 floor collapses 1-2, 1-3, 0-2, 0-3 and 0-4 onto
one value. Inside an equal-points group, rounds played never reaches the floor.

rank_standings now accepts the OMW map it would otherwise build, so a caller
that displays the tiebreak passes the same map it prints. get_standings_with_omw
was deriving it twice per load -- 46% of that function's compute, and paid by
every caller that discards it -- and the two copies agreed only because both
call sites happened to carry identical arguments.

 DraftBot: read the league page's standings from the shared loader 

 …

 b475e2c 

 The page re-queried the swiss match graph and re-derived OMW% itself, keeping a
second copy of "swiss rounds only" spelled as a bare string rather than
STAGE_PLAYOFF -- the divergence between the two surfaces this module exists to
prevent. get_standings_with_omw already returns both from one load.

Also: the cut rule is named after a cut, so it is drawn only when one is
declared, rather than rendering "top None cut"; and the standings board gains a
test for a dropped team sitting inside the cut, where the seatable rank and the
cut size part company. Both existing cut tests used values where the two
coincide, so passing cut_to in place of the rank left the suite green.
